title: The rows a harness stores for a run, and what it replays, in three languages
pins: The rows each language writes for an assistant turn and a tool result turn, including tool call arguments, provider ids and state, approval requests and approval decisions, the parsed document a structured turn stores beside its text, the row a runner start writes when it ends the calls a child was parked on, and the view a stored run is replayed as. A PHP app and a TypeScript or Python agent can share one session. If one language keys an approval to a call differently, it resumes another language's approval against the wrong call or never. If one stores an empty map as a list, a typed reader refuses the row. If one replays consecutive tool result rows unfolded, a provider receives a tool output twice or an empty turn it refuses. If one marks an ended call differently, or not at all, or reads the mark only on the first result row that carries the call id, it reads a call another language ended (never ran) as approved, and the decision stands for a side effect that never happened.
scope: Row SHAPE: key names, key order, and the JSON type of empty maps, for the assistant and tool_result rows the harness runtime records, and the fold of consecutive tool result rows applied on replay; and (0.3.0, G-387) the row a runner start records when it ends the calls a child was parked on (thr-0014): one fixed result per call with no result in the last tool-calling step, and the harness-only `harness_ended_by_start: {approval_ids: [...]}` mark after `tool_approval_responses`, naming the approvals in CALL order. Calls in one step that share a tool_call_id are NOT in this row (G-392). And (0.4.0, G-387 round 13) one READ, pinned by thr-0015 with `read: approval_states`: over rows as stored, whether each approval reads ended by a runner start, which is true exactly when a result row after its own request and before the next assistant row carries the mark naming it. NOT user rows (their attachments are pinned by harness-turn-attachments and media-roundtrip), NOT the approval RESOLUTION logic (which calls run on resume; each language's own tests drive that, the PHP reference through real provider handlers), NOT how a client maps rows onto a provider's wire format, and and NOT rows written by earlier port releases, which the ports read and the reference never wrote. User rows are out of scope BY DECISION, not because they agree: a draft case carrying them found that PHP writes `additional_content` and `additional_attributes` as empty LISTS on a plain user turn where both ports write neither key. That is recorded under G-58 in the envelope's port gaps register rather than pinned here, because widening a suite's scope to hold a finding hides which question the suite actually asks. And (0.5.0, G-387 round 14) two more FOLD rows: two calls of one step that share a tool call id but not their tool or arguments each keep their own result on replay (thr-0016, G-403), and a step's results are replayed once per segment even when its result rows are not consecutive (thr-0017: a resolution recorded after a system row carries the step's earlier results again; the replay leaves the repeats out, the first stands where it was). And (0.5.1, G-387 round 15) a `place` kind over rows AS STORED (a row the harness wrote carries `harness: true`): the replay honours the harness's `harness_answers_step {position}` mark only on such rows and only when it names an earlier step with that call (thr-0018, a host tool-call step recorded while a run resolves a call; thr-0020, a forged mark on a host row changes nothing), never sends a started row and reads a started call with no result as interrupted (thr-0019), reads a row whose tool_calls hold no object as a text row and an earlier step left with no outcome as replaced (thr-0021), and replays the decision that stands, a denial over an approval, with a later step's repeated approval request asking for nothing (thr-0024); and two write rows, the write-ahead started row (thr-0022) and a step whose approval requests are bound to their calls by tool name and canonical-arguments digest (thr-0023). And (0.6.0, G-387 round 16) ONE trust signal: a harness mark is read only on a row the runtime wrote (`harness: true`); a run id is never one, and every mark on any other row reads as absent (thr-0033, thr-0034; thr-0015's ended row now carries `harness: true`). The decision that STANDS for an approval is one recorded while its call had no outcome, a denial over an approval, and the replay shows only it (thr-0028, thr-0029; thr-0009 changed deliberately: a later approval recorded after call_2's outcome never stood). Every call of a step no longer paused with no outcome gets one in the replay, replaced if it was requested, else interrupted, and an ungated call's started row (approval_id null) reads interrupted (thr-0030, thr-0031); a newer step parked by another run is left open (thr-0032). A new write `answer` (thr-0025: only the new results) and two reads, `call_outcomes` (thr-0026, thr-0027: a result answers the first call with no outcome) and `approval_reads` (thr-0035: pending and the standing decision).
findings: Thirteen rows agree, and seven of them did not when the corpus was first run: the reference stored an assistant turn with no provider state as `"additional_content":[]`, an empty list, where both ports store `{}`. The reference moved (prism-harness MessageMapper now stores a map). The ports' earlier releases wrote tool calls with an id and a name only, tool results one row per call, and approvals in rows of their own, so every write row in this corpus would have disagreed with them. thr-0014 (0.3.0, G-387) was added because a review found the three languages writing three different ended marks, none reading another's: the shape is the PHP reference's, and the ports write and read exactly it. The three structured-turn rows (thr-0011..0013, added 2026-09-20 with G-61) agreed on the first run, which is the uncommon outcome here and is explained by the ports being written against this shape rather than discovered to share it. Agreement licenses one conclusion: the three languages store and replay a run in the same shape, so a thread written by one reads the same in the others. It says nothing about whether the decisions stored in it were authorised, which is the application's to check before recording them. thr-0015 (0.4.0, G-387 round 13) pins a READ, not a row: a review found that the reference and both ports read the ended mark only on the FIRST result row carrying the call id, so on a step whose calls share an id, an earlier unmarked result of the sibling call hid the start's mark and a person's decision stood for a call that never ran. All three languages shared it, so no comparison could have shown it; the case was written from the rule, and the reference before its round-13 change reads apr_1 there as not ended. thr-0016 and thr-0017 (0.5.0, G-387 round 14) were written from the rule. thr-0016 agreed with the reference already (its fold keys by id, tool name and arguments since round 13b) and pins the TypeScript and Python folds, which keyed by call id alone. thr-0017 is a defect the reference shared: its fold merged only CONSECUTIVE result rows, so a resolution recorded after a system row replayed a result twice. thr-0018..thr-0024 (0.5.1, G-387 round 15) were written from the rule (the write-ahead started row, the approval binding, one step rule, a denial is final); the reference produced them first and the ports reproduce them. thr-0025..thr-0035 (0.6.0, G-387 round 16) were written from the rule; the reference produced them first. thr-0009's expected value changed deliberately in 0.6.0 (the replay's decision fold was last-wins).
